beginner: Oil prices have surged more than 25% in a single week after the US-Israel war on Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, the world's most critical oil shipping lane. WTI crude hit $90.90 and Brent reached $92.69 per barrel.

Gold has reached new all-time highs above $5,100 per ounce as investors rush to safe-haven assets amid the Middle East conflict and global market uncertainty — a significant boost for gold-mining countries like South Africa.

Natural gas prices are sharply higher after Iranian drone strikes forced Qatar — the world's largest LNG exporter — to declare force majeure and halt operations, cutting off about 20% of global liquefied natural gas supply.
moderate: WTI Crude at $90.90/barrel (+36% WoW) and Brent at $92.69 (+27%) reflect acute Strait of Hormuz disruption: ~140 million barrels of regional crude is stranded, OPEC+ announced a larger-than-expected production increase but barrels are largely inaccessible given the shipping halt; analysts warn Brent could exceed $100 if the conflict lasts beyond 4 weeks.

Gold at $5,158/oz continues its multi-year bull run, now compounded by the Iran conflict flight-to-safety bid; the metal benefits simultaneously from central bank buying (EM reserve diversification), USD weakness earlier in 2026, and an acute geopolitical risk premium; silver at $84.31 is tracking higher on both safe-haven and industrial demand.

Agricultural commodities are rising as the Middle East conflict disrupts shipping: wheat (+5.8% weekly) faces a dual shock — the Middle East is a large wheat importer and key shipping routes are disrupted; soybeans (+3.2%) are supported by China's continued import demand and Brazilian export strength; corn (+4.3%) reflects biofuel demand as energy prices spike globally.
expert: The WTI/Brent spread has narrowed to ~$1.79 (from a typical $3-5), reflecting the global nature of the supply shock and US SPR release speculation: with approximately 9mb/d off the market from facility damage and precautionary shutdowns, and OPEC+ production geographically constrained by Hormuz closure, the market's clearing mechanism is IEA strategic reserve coordination — a tool that buys weeks, not months, of price suppression.

Gold's rally above $5,100 represents a regime shift in the gold-real-rate relationship: previously gold tracked inversely to US real rates (TIPS yields); the current gold strength despite higher real rates (driven by CPI upside from energy) suggests the safe-haven bid is overriding the rate-discount mechanism — a pattern historically associated with tail-risk scenarios where the monetary policy reaction function itself becomes uncertain.

Agricultural commodity supercycle dynamics are being reinforced by the Iran shock: fertiliser (natural gas-intensive in production) prices are spiking with LNG, creating a second-order agricultural supply shock for the 2026/2027 growing season; the FAO food price index is likely to reverse its recent moderation; and the combination of energy and food price inflation in a single shock is historically the most damaging inflation configuration for EM sovereign credit.

commentary.beginner: Commodities are the raw materials that power the global economy - things like oil, gold, wheat, and copper. Their prices affect everything from the cost of filling your car to the price of bread. When oil rises, transport gets more expensive, which pushes up prices across the board. Gold often rises when people are worried about the economy.
commentary.moderate: Commodity markets are signalling mixed conditions. Energy prices remain subdued on soft China demand and resilient US shale supply, while gold continues to rally on central bank buying and safe-haven demand. Agricultural commodities are pressured by strong Southern Hemisphere harvests. The copper-to-gold ratio - a classic growth proxy - has been declining, consistent with a slowing global cycle.
commentary.expert: Cross-commodity signal extraction: the backwardation in crude (WTI M1-M6 spread ~$1.80) suggests physical tightness despite flat prices, consistent with OPEC+ compliance above 90%. Gold's move above $2,900 is driven less by real rates (still positive) and more by EM central bank reserve diversification (PBOC, RBI, NBP cumulative buying ~1,100t in 2024-25). Dr. Copper's sideways action reflects offsetting forces: China property drag vs. electrification pull. The GSCI/SPX ratio near 40-year lows signals extreme undervaluation of real assets vs. financial assets.

beginner.label: Iran Conflict Shocks Energy Markets
beginner.body: The US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28, triggering the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and cutting off about 20% of the world's oil supply. Oil prices have jumped over 25% in a week, raising fuel costs for households and businesses everywhere.

beginner.label: Central Banks Caught in Stagflation Trap
beginner.body: Many central banks around the world had been preparing to cut interest rates to support their economies, but the sudden oil price shock from the Middle East is forcing them to reconsider — higher energy costs could push inflation back up while growth slows simultaneously.

beginner.label: Shipping Lanes Disrupted Worldwide
beginner.body: With the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed to tanker traffic, ships carrying oil, gas, and goods are being rerouted at much greater cost and delay. Countries in Asia and Europe that rely on Middle East energy are most affected, and Qatar has declared force majeure on its huge LNG exports.

moderate.label: Hormuz Closure: 20% of Global Oil Offline
moderate.body: The US-Israel war on Iran (Day 8) has effectively halted tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, stranding ~140 million barrels of regional oil and pushing WTI to $90.90/barrel (+36% WoW) and Brent to $92.69 (+27%). Qatar declared LNG force majeure after drone strikes on its gas facilities, removing ~20% of global LNG supply from the market.

moderate.label: Fed, ECB, BoE All Frozen by Energy Shock
moderate.body: Markets have rapidly repriced central bank rate paths: Fed June cut probability near zero (July-September earliest), BoE March cut probability collapsed from 84% to 30%, and the ECB faces a 'genuine dilemma' as energy inflation and weak growth pull policy in opposite directions. The oil shock could add 0.8pp to global inflation if sustained.

moderate.label: Supply Chain Disruption Spreading Beyond Oil
moderate.body: The Hormuz closure is rippling through non-energy supply chains: India's basmati rice exports (400,000 metric tons) are stuck at ports, fertiliser prices are spiking with LNG, airspace closures are grounding cargo flights across the Gulf, and European diesel prices have doubled in a week. The IMF has put global growth under review.

expert.label: Hormuz Shock: Structural vs. Transitory Energy Risk
expert.body: The key macro question is duration: a 2-4 week Hormuz closure keeps Brent at $80-90 with manageable passthrough (~0.5pp global CPI). A sustained 3-month+ closure pushes Brent above $100, adds 0.8pp to global inflation, and materially impairs the Fed/ECB/BoE rate-cutting cycles. Iran's targeting of regional energy infrastructure (Qatar LNG, Saudi refinery, Kuwait precautionary shutdown) suggests damage extending well beyond any ceasefire timeline.
expert.source: Bank of America / Rystad Energy / Bloomberg, March 2026

expert.label: Global Monetary Policy: The Stagflation Trilemma
expert.body: Central banks face a trilemma: a supply-shock-driven CPI spike with simultaneously weakening aggregate demand and deteriorating financial conditions means neither rate hikes nor cuts are unambiguously correct. The Nomura framework calls for 'fiscal-first' response — price controls, subsidies, excise cuts — before monetary policy reacts; but this worsens fiscal positions already under stress from pre-Iran deficit levels.

expert.label: Geopolitical Fragmentation Accelerates
expert.body: The Iran conflict is the third major geopolitical shock in three years (Russia/Ukraine 2022, Gaza 2023, Iran 2026) and may permanently accelerate deglobalisation: Asian economies are rerouting supply chains, Gulf producers are reassessing the USD petrodollar arrangement, and the US military's dual commitment in Ukraine and the Middle East is straining strategic bandwidth. BlackRock's March 2026 note identifies geopolitical fragmentation as the dominant long-run driver of asset price dispersion.
